articles.title: Ireland’s Matches Against Israel Should Have Been Canceled
articles.author: Luan Rogers
articles.content: On Sunday night, the Irish soccer team bowed their heads in silence as the Israeli anthem echoed through the all but empty Nagyerdei Stadium in Debrecen, Hungary’s second-largest city. The Irish players, who wore black armbands, skipped the traditional pregame rituals. There were no handshakes, no pennants, and (for the most part) no fans. After months of deliberations and growing demands for a boycott, these trite gestures of dissent were all the Irish team could muster. Having spurned an opportunity to set an international precedent, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) succumbed to fear, meekly agreeing to go through with the matches. This was a decision that the Irish players had seemed destined to glumly accept until some final deliberations nearly scuttled the ship at the eleventh hour. In the end, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu opted to take a one-man stand after a truly dramatic day for Irish soccer. The evolution of this match into a contentious diplomatic high-wire act demonstrates the full extent of Israel’s international isolation. Nonetheless, the saga ultimately reveals how, despite ardent public support, fears of punitive action continue to undermine Irish support for Palestine. From Dublin to Debrecen Israel selected Hungary as the location of its Nations League clash against Ireland, the site of nearly all its “home” internationals since October 7, 2023. Although the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) did not allocate away tickets for Irish fans, a dozen or so diehards managed to enter the stadium to offer their support. Not only were Irish fans effectively blocked from attending, but the national broadcaster, Raidió Teilifís Éireann (RTÉ), also decided to strip back its coverage to the bare minimum. Television viewership dropped below its usual levels as fans across the country staged mini-boycotts of their own. The shrill blast of the opening whistle ultimately brought down the curtain on a failed boycott campaign that had gripped the country for months. At this late stage, the very fact that the game was even happening seemed to overshadow the importance of its actual outcome. At the end of an admittedly challenging week, Ireland took out their frustration on their opponents from the start, amassing a three–nil lead in the space of just twenty-five minutes. After scoring Ireland’s third and final goal, Jack Moylan removed his black armband and kissed it in front of the Israeli fans in an apparent gesture of Palestinian solidarity. No number of goals or pointed celebrations could dampen the spirit of the hundred or so Israeli fans who had made the pilgrimage to Hungary. Regardless of the result, they seemed to be celebrating the mere fact that the game had gone ahead. A Pyrrhic Victory Even after their team had gone three goals down, the Israeli supporters continued to chant in support of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). In a video recorded from the stands, Yoseph Haddad, a far-right Israeli activist, proclaimed that while Ireland might have won, “they will never, ever break the Israeli spirit.” The Israeli fans reportedly directed racist abuse at one of Ireland’s goal scorers, Adam Idah. UEFA have since declined to investigate the incident on the basis that the Irish players did not properly report it. This appears to mean that while Idah’s teammate Jayson Molumby asked the match officials to listen to the chanting, he did not specifically mention the word “racism.” As the game wore on, tempers frayed. Various on-field scuffles later culminated in an alleged changing room melee between Irish defender Jake O’Brien and Israeli captain Manor Solomon. The hostility continued well after the final whistle. In a post-match outburst, Solomon boasted to reporters that “we have a country that is ten times better than theirs.” When asked about the Irish players, the former IDF soldier said that he would probably be suspended if he stated his opinion in full: “Obviously they hate us, and we don’t like them.” Ireland, who have not won a competitive game by this margin in over three years, sliced through the Israeli defense with uncharacteristic precision. Any satisfaction came with a nagging sense of guilt, knowing that any victory pales in comparison to what could have been gained by a full-fledged boycott. Bypassing the Boycott As soon as UEFA announced the Nations League draw back in February, many Irish fans mobilized behind the boycott campaign. On the eve of Sunday’s game, over 160 Irish sports figures had signed an open letter urging the team to stop the game. With public pressure mounting, the FAI opted to play Ireland’s second game against Israel, which was due to take place in Dublin, at a small stadium in rural Serbia instead, citing “security concerns” as a rationale. The FAI’s decision essentially denied Irish fans the chance to directly picket any of the games. Within the Irish football community, the debate has created a rift between the grassroots and those at the institutional level. A broad coalition of fans, players, and coaches from the domestic league has come out strongly against the FAI’s decision. War of Words The FAI officials responsible for the decision to play seemed keen to avoid the spotlight and left the team’s Icelandic head coach, Heimir Hallgrímson, to bear the brunt of public scrutiny. The Israel Football Association launched an extraordinary attack on Hallgrímson after he made the following statement in the run-up to the game: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide. We are playing against Israel; we are not playing with Israel.” There can be few if any precedents in modern sporting history for the Israel FA’s official response : We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way. Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by the Republic of Ireland team coach. We’re not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we’re playing against the coach who embodies them. This put paid to any notion that it was possible to keep politics out of sport in this situation. However, the FAI did not see it as an opportunity to revisit their decision to play the games. Nor did they see any need to publicly defend Hallgrímson. The Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, did intervene on his behalf, branding the Israeli remarks “unacceptable” and calling for them to be withdrawn: “Israel can’t keep denying what the world knows, and what the world understands.” But there was no statement from the FAI, although it was reported to have complained to UEFA privately. The FAI could easily have stated that Hallgrímson was using the word “genocide” because this is the official position of the Irish government, which has decided to join the South African case at the International Court of Justice, accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention through its actions in Gaza. It could also have briefed Hallgrímson to make the same point in his defense. There appears to have been no effort to do so. Ill-equipped to handle the political weight of the situation, the former dentist wilted in the line of fire at the pre-match press conference. Hallgrímson fielded questions from combative Israeli journalists, hounding him over a past coaching position in Qatar as well as Ireland’s decision to play against Nazi Germany in the 1930s. Under pressure, he apologized for using the word “genocide” in his previous statement: “It is a strong word and the wrong word for me to use.” Hallgrímson’s capitulation seemed only to embolden the Israel FA, which flippantly declared, after Ireland agreed to play, that “football had won.” Israel FA Head of Communications Shlomi Barzel was asked if he was responsible for the statement that charged Hallgrímson with “stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy.” His response was defiant: “I am responsible for that, and I am not going to apologize. After hearing him today, I will take back the word ‘stupidity.’” In other words, he stood by his description of the Ireland manager as an ignorant hypocrite. Uncomfortable Position With most of the public discontent directed at both the FAI and the Irish government, recent protests had started to target the players themselves. Activists had picketed the team’s Dublin hotel before they departed for their upcoming games. After the team suffered an ignominious defeat to Kosovo a few days beforehand, Irish midfielder Jason Knight became the first player to state that the games against Israel should not go ahead. Others, such as Chiedozie Ogbene, later vented their frustration, urging the public “not to put pressure on us.” As uncertainty spread through the camp, news broke on Saturday that goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu would be withdrawing from the match-day squad. He issued a statement explaining his motivations: My decision is based purely upon my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong. It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community but against the atrocities in the region. There are few times where you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger and I strongly believe this is one of them. Reporters camped outside the hotel as Irish players deliberated on whether to go ahead with the game. Former Ireland manager Brian Kerr, who has been a vocal supporter of the boycott campaign, was in touch with Bazunu. He reported that a vote was held with Bazunu absent, with the players voting 14–8 in favor of going ahead. The FAI declined to confirm or deny the exact figures, merely referring to a “significant majority” among the players. Having had months to establish a firm stance, the FAI haplessly equivocated. According to Brian Kerr, Bazunu was left “feeling quite low and shunned by some of the players and by the FAI” after his decision. Seemingly immune to the chorus of criticism, FAI President Paul Cooke later claimed that the situation “went as well as could be expected in the face of unprecedented coverage.” Opposition parties have since called on the FAI leadership to step down in the wake of the fiasco. Fear of Retribution The FAI cited the threat of disciplinary action in support of its decision not to boycott the matches. The decision also comes against the backdrop of Ireland cohosting the 2028 European Championship — the country’s first time staging a major tournament. In a bulletin distributed to FAI members at a July extraordinary general meeting (EGM), the association suggested that Ireland could be suspended from future competitions in the event of a boycott. Further estimations of a potential $10.3 million loss of revenue seem overblown in the light of other recent boycott actions. Since 2024, Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia have all refused to play various women’s and underage matches against Belarus, citing the country’s ongoing involvement in the Ukraine war. UEFA docked the Baltic teams no more than three points each, and in one instance dished out a €5,000 fine. After the match on Sunday, the FAI’s Paul Cooke referred to the exclusion of Southampton from the promotion playoffs for the English Championship earlier this year as an example of what might have happened to Ireland in the event of a boycott. But the two situations could hardly be less similar: Southampton were punished for spying on the training sessions of their rivals. The Irish players may have also been subjected to other forms of external pressure. Several well-informed sources passed on rumors that some players were told by their agents that they might be blacklisted from playing for English clubs with American owners if they chose not to play. Inconsistent Action Although they reject ed the boycott at the July EGM, FAI members voted overwhelmingly last November to submit a motion calling for Israel’s suspension from UEFA. This obvious contradiction demonstrates how institutional support for Palestine does not yet outweigh the perceived costs of unilateral action. Under similar circumstances in 1999, Ireland chose to boycott a European qualifier against Yugoslavia because of atrocities carried out in Kosovo. The FAI avoided expulsion from the European Championship, receiving only a moderate fine from UEFA. Norway, which hosted Israel in a World Cup qualifier earlier last year, has spearheaded the campaign to suspend Israel from UEFA. Its officials have drawn comparisons with the ban on Russian national and club teams that UEFA imposed soon after the invasion of Ukraine began. Following the recent controversy, the FAI asked that Ireland and Israel be separated from future group stage pairings. UEFA denied the request on the basis that the two nations “have never been in direct conflict.” Cognitive Dissonance The ongoing controversy has unfolded against the backdrop of Ireland’s increasingly strained relations with Israel. The Irish government has imposed travel bans on two far-right Israeli ministers and recently moved to prohibit the import of goods from Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territories. Ireland’s heavy reliance on US investment leaves it potentially vulnerable to pressure from Washington. Before his recent death, Republican Senator Lindsey Graham threatened that countries that “participate in the effort to marginalize Israel in sports” would “pay a heavy price when it comes to access to the American economy.” The Occupied Territories Bill had promised to be a groundbreaking piece of legislation when first proposed to the Irish parliament in 2018. After extensive deliberations, the government eventually passed a diluted version of the bill earlier this year, which excluded trade in services from the ban. Despite otherwise advocating for international sanctions on Israel, the Irish government has supported the FAI’s decision to participate in the games. “We don’t want to damage ourselves unnecessarily,” cautioned Micheál Martin. In a separate interview , he argued that “sport is an area that can be challenging when it crosses into the realm of politics.” Martin’s comments echo the rhetoric of international soccer bodies that extol the sport’s power to unite people while approaching contentious political issues with caution if not cowardice. Amid demands for Israel’s suspension, FIFA President Gianni Infantino has said that “football cannot solve geopolitical problems,” instead summoning its “power to bring people together in a divided world.” At FIFA’s annual congress this year, Infantino tried to organize a now infamous photo op between Israeli and Palestinian delegates. The toe-curling gaffe followed a passionate speech by the Palestinian representative in which he called for sanctions against Israel over the formation of soccer clubs in the occupied territories. Looking Ahead Although the decisive nature of the victory may have restored some public faith in the team, it remains to be seen how the fans will receive the players when they take on Austria in Dublin today. The match comes just days before the second clash against Israel in Serbia. The FAI has already moved fans with pitch-side seats in anticipation of further protest action. Ireland’s last home game, a May friendly against Qatar, featured a demonstration in which fans threw tennis balls with printed Palestine flags onto the pitch. In what briefly promised to be the dawn of a new era in the global campaign to boycott Israel, the limits of Irish institutional support for Palestine have become clear. Without coordinated multilateral action involving other associations, the FAI seems unlikely to lead by example, particularly under its current gutless leadership. Despite the best efforts of those leaders to isolate sports from politics, this contentious match proves that the two are inseparable, if not integral to each other. With the FAI’s credibility all but erased, it’s left to the players once again to make a decision. articles.title: Frederick Douglass Had a Radical Respect for the Constitution
articles.author: Bradley Rebeiro
articles.content: Is the US Constitution for or against slavery? Questions concerning the legacy of America’s founding and how to interpret the Constitution have long gripped public discourse; in recent years they have become inseparable. From the 1980s came the originalists, a group of legal theorists who sought to recover the Constitution’s original meaning through textual analysis buttressed by historical investigation. Adhering to the document’s original meaning, they argue, promotes institutional stability and the rule of law. Scholars have long contested these claims, challenging the plausibility of recovering an “original meaning” or doubting the authoritative nature of such meaning even if discovered. Recently, however, a second phenomenon has brought constitutional discourse closer to political discourse. The 1619 Project has inspired new attacks against the originalist normative claim, as it recasts the nation’s history in terms of its legacy as a slaveholding nation committed to white supremacy. Scholars are now challenging originalism on the grounds that it is part and parcel of a tradition of oppression that cannot demand a people’s loyalty, much less respect. This reframes the question from the accessibility of original meaning and its authoritative nature to the problem of original meaning as it relates to constitutional evils. Still, originalists continue to defend the founding of the United States as a moment that instilled constitutional norms worth preserving. Indeed, they are compelled to do so. Originalism would not be worth its salt — promoting stability and the rule of law — if it meant only preserving oppression and white supremacy. Increasingly, we find two historical accounts representing two mutually exclusive Americas: an America founded on perpetuating slavery and white supremacy versus an America dedicated to liberty and equality. This clash of narratives is hardly new. The antebellum period was rife with political disputes concerning the future of slavery. Proslavery and antislavery advocates alike turned to the past to measure America as it was against what it should be. Slavery’s defenders argued that the institution was a positive good and that the framers of the Constitution enshrined protections for it. Fidelity to the founding of the nation, in their view, required protecting slavery as an indispensable American institution. Antislavery advocates, alternatively, argued that the Constitution did not recognize slavery as a positive good but set it on a course for eventual extinction. Defenders of slavery and antislavery advocates used conflicting interpretive frameworks to justify their respective understandings of the Constitution’s treatment of slavery. As is the case in the present day, both narratives posited conflicting accounts concerning history and its authoritative grip on the present. Still, both sides recognized that, at some level, one could not chart a course for a future that had no regard for the debt owed to the past. Frederick Douglass’s Alternative There is one figure in history who is uniquely positioned to shed light on complex nineteenth-century constitutional development and to speak to our current constitutional-political moment: Frederick Douglass, the former slave turned radical activist turned statesman. Modern-day critics and proponents of the Constitution’s beginnings alike reference the controversial conclusion in his famous speech “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” that the Constitution was a “GLORIOUS LIBERTY DOCUMENT.” In that speech, Douglass has many rhetorical flourishes that either side might find useful in vindicating its position on the Constitution. Those who seek to salvage the Constitution from its relationship with slavery hold Douglass up as paradigmatic of proper veneration of the Constitution. Those who seek to malign the Constitution’s beginnings tend to focus on his scathing rebuke of America — in the very same speech — as his true message. Any reference to the Constitution or the Founders in positive terms, they argue, is nothing more than a rhetorical device aimed at increasing the potency of Douglass’s censure of the nation. But both groups fail to seriously consider the method behind his conclusion. What both accounts miss is that Douglass has much more to offer concerning constitutional fidelity and constitutional interpretation than his “Fourth of July” speech. Constitutional fidelity is not to be blindly adhered to; nor is it merely a pragmatic consideration. The Constitution is truly good when correctly interpreted. Douglass’s constitutional thought uniquely answered the question of what the Constitution’s posture toward slavery was. While some abolitionists simply accepted slavery as an indelible blemish on the Constitution, Douglass sought to redeem the Constitution from the evils of slavery. Indeed, he helped constitutional abolitionists popularize a natural rights theory of interpretation that excised slavery from the Constitution. Through this interpretation, he sought to put all persons on equal footing before the law. His great task, as he described it, was “by voice and pen . . . to stand for the freedom of people of all colors, until in our land the last yoke was broken and the last bondsman was set free.” His approach to the Constitution was critical in that endeavor, and it contributed to burgeoning constitutional thought in the antebellum period. Douglass was a cardinal figure during one of the most consequential moments in US constitutional development. He was a direct participant in the antebellum debate over slavery, which set in motion several theories of constitutional interpretation. Though methods and conclusions varied, each side of the debate claimed fidelity to the Constitution through an appeal to its text and to history. These debates shaped constitutional thought during the antebellum period and carried over into public deliberation during Reconstruction. Among the throng of opinions, we find Douglass arguing that based on the text, history, and natural rights, the Constitution was resolutely antislavery. His method was based primarily on natural rights principles. He argued that the Founders built this nation on a natural rights foundation, the principles of which were pronounced in the Declaration of Independence. As such, one had to interpret the Constitution according to those natural rights principles. But studying Douglass provides more than an arresting theory of constitutional interpretation. His intellectual journey is fascinating: he discovered for himself the significance of the nation’s founding principles after having survived harrowing experiences of cruelty and oppression under the color of law. Insufficient attention is given to just how exceptional Douglass was. After he escaped to freedom, he ventured into the world of the antislavery movement. There he quickly found fellowship with William Lloyd Garrison, an experience-hardened abolitionist who famously referred to the Constitution as “a covenant with death, and an agreement with hell.” Garrison and his camp, relying on James Madison’s Notes of Debates in the Federal Convention of 1787 , argued incessantly that the Constitution was irredeemably a proslavery document and that the Union, by extension, was a curse. This left the Garrisonians only one possibility: the abolition of slavery meant disunion and abolishing the Constitution along with it. At first, Douglass adopted these views without reservation; he spoke at antislavery conventions across the North, disparaging the framers, cursing the founding, and expressing nothing but contempt for the Constitution. Douglass’s inquisitive and capacious mind could not long be satisfied with received wisdom, however. In a short time, he abandoned the Garrisonian position. As he consulted more accounts of the founding and the Constitution, Douglass became convinced that the Constitution was in fact an antislavery document, and that the truest interpretation of it would require abolishing slavery for the sake of union. Most look to him for his exceptional oratory skills, which have withstood the test of time, and rightfully so. Yet lurking under his witty remarks and fierce retorts attacking the power of the slave-owning class rested a cogent theory of law and legal interpretation. Douglass also offers a lesson for political actors who must confront the tension between their own theories and the demands of politics. Rarely does history provide an example of a figure with an intellectual stature comparable to Douglass and place that figure at the center of great constitutional change. He had a robust theory of law and justice that guided his actions during the antebellum period. It was only during Reconstruction, however, that political realities forced Douglass to act in ways that did not always reflect his theory. Douglass believed that the United States would be “complete” only when it granted equal rights to all its citizens, and especially universal suffrage. At the time, this meant expanding the circle of democratic participation to African Americans and women. But after early defeats in Reconstruction, it became clear to Douglass that there was insufficient political will to extend suffrage to both groups. Douglass’s natural rights constitutionalism had a clear answer for what the nation needed to do, but ideas alone could not bring a constitutional amendment into being. Confronted with the political exigencies of Reconstruction, Douglass pushed for African American suffrage at the expense of women’s suffrage to move the arc of justice forward. Douglass calculated the move to be an unfortunate but necessary one. As soon as the Fifteenth Amendment — which guaranteed suffrage regardless of race — was ratified, Douglass went to work again in favor of women’s suffrage. Indeed, he proves an excellent exemplar of the timeless question of prudence when confronted with this tension between theory and practice. For these reasons, Douglass remains relevant for Americans today. He teaches us much about our past and how to confront it in a sober but hopeful way. He also teaches us something of what it means to traverse adversity for the sake of justice, and how it at times might require momentary sacrifice for long-term gains. Douglass preserves the legacy of the Constitution in favor of freedom and provides a method for ensuring the Constitution delivers a brighter tomorrow. articles.title: Protests sweep India demanding removal of Chief Election Commissioner
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Nationwide protests have broken out in India this week seeking the removal of the country’s Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) over allegations of irregularities in the electoral process during various state elections and the deliberate mass disenfranchisement in favor of the ultra-right-wing ruling dispensation. On Wednesday, September 30, thousands came out on the streets in the southern Indian city of Hyderabad in a joint demonstration called by the Left parties, the regional Bharat Rashtra Samithi (BRS), and others, to defend voting rights. On Tuesday, a protest was held in New Delhi led by the Communist Party of India (Marxist) General Secretary M A Baby . The protesters, who were marching to the Election Commission of India (ECI) headquarters, were detained by the security forces for hours in an attempt to disrupt the march. Similar protests have been held in different parts of the country by various other groups and political formations, including the main opposition party, the Indian National Congress (INC), the civil society groups, student and youth organizations, and the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP). The CJP, which successfully led a protest by students and youth in the country earlier this year against the union government’s education policies, has called for another national mobilization over the issue beginning on October 2. The protesters have listed three major demands: halting the so-called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls the re-inclusion of all the voters removed so far from the electoral rolls the removal of the CEC Mr. Gyanesh Kumar Protestors say these demands are essential to protect the fundamental right to vote, currently at risk by the Chief Election Commissioner. Read more: India’s Cockroach Rebellion and what comes next Over 130 million removed from the electoral rolls India does not have a centralized electoral roll. They are prepared at the local constituency levels. The CEC in the country has been accused of changing this by arbitrarily changing rules and initiating processes. The opposition alleges these actions were taken in order to have control over the electoral outcome. According to the data compiled by various reports, over 130 million voters have been deleted from the electoral rolls of different states in India, citing various reasons since the so-called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) began last year. Reports indicate that in several state legislative constituencies, the number of voters deleted from the electoral rolls were more than the victory margins during the elections. Despite its large electoral base, in India’s First Past the Poll system, margins of victory in state legislative constituencies are often very small, ranging from a few to a few thousand votes. It has also been reported that because of the SIR, in some smaller states between one third to half of all voters have been deleted or put into doubtful lists by the ECI. In bigger states such as Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal, millions of people have been excluded. In most of these cases, those removed from the electoral list have either already missed their opportunity to vote or expected to miss it given the slow process of appeals for re-inclusion. For example, in West Bengal, elections were held earlier this year with millions of citizens failing to exercise their right to vote while waiting for the re-inclusion of their names in the electoral list. The majority of those who failed to reapply and get their names back into the electoral rolls in time are from economically marginalized sections or from the Muslim-minority communities. The ECI has also been accused of deliberately suppressing crucial information from the public and delaying the proceedings. A deliberate move to benefit the ruling party The opposition has been accusing that these deletions and the slow process of appeals are deliberate moves adopted by the ECI in complete violation of the country’s legal and constitutional provisions. The process disregards citizens’ fundamental right to vote, the opposition claims. Opposition parties, civil society groups, and others have been protesting against the process since the beginning while claiming that the process was invented to manipulate the elections in favor of the ruling ultra-right-wing and Hindu supremacist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Civil society groups and some political parties also filed a petition in the country’s Supreme Court last year challenging the SIR. However, the process has continued as the court has repeatedly refused to stay it. The top court’s refusal to stay the SIR despite acknowledging irregularities and violations in its execution from time to time has enraged the opposition parties and civil society activists. The current upsurge was a result of a report published in the Indian Express , one of India’s leading English daily papers on September 23. The report, citing official documents, exposed that the CEC Mr. Kumar bypassed the majority objections and made unilateral decisions related to the SIR on at least 14 occasions. There are two more commissioners apart from the CEC in the ECI all appointed by the union government. The laws clearly state that all decisions in the ECI must be taken either by a consensus or by a majority. Mr. Kumar’s unilateral decisions related to the SIR process, including the rules regarding voter enrollment, the deletion or inclusion of names in the electoral rolls, among others, have unfairly benefited the ruling party, including in West Bengal, which amounts to stealing the elections, the opposition alleges. The BJP came to power in West Bengal, one of India’s largest provinces, for the first time earlier this year amidst allegations of the deliberate exclusion of millions of voters from the electoral rolls. On Tuesday, the INC issued a statement calling for more protests across the nation and reiterating the demands for Mr. Kumar’s removal, apart from the immediate halt of the SIR and the re-inclusion of all the voters wrongfully deleted from the electoral rolls. Second freedom struggle The INC has alleged that the irregularities in the electoral process are nothing less than “a theft of votes and democracy” done by the ECI under the leadership of Mr. Kumar on behalf of the ruling BJP and the movement will not stop until he is removed from his post and tried for his criminal actions. It also claimed that the movement for the restoration of the right of all adult citizens to vote is no less than a second “freedom struggle,” invoking India’s anti-colonial movement against the British in the early twentieth century. All the left parties, led by the CPI (M), also issued a joint statement last week seeking the removal of Mr. Kumar, and the withdrawal of the SIR process, claiming the allegations against him raise serious questions regarding the constitutional protection of the right to vote and elect representatives. The SIR, under Mr. Kumar’s leadership in the ECI, has created doubts about the fairness and integrity of the electoral process in India, the Left parties said, claiming it needs to be urgently corrected.

articles.title: AI’s real crisis: the $4 trillion bet that could crash the US economy
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: Is the AI bubble about to burst? Tech giants like Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are betting over $4 trillion on data centers, chips, and AI models – but the profits aren’t there yet, and the cash is running out. Michael Roberts, economist and author of The Next Recession blog, joins Zoe Alexandra to break down the reality behind the AI boom – what he calls the biggest economic gamble in US history – and who will pay the price when the house of cards comes down. Roberts explains how circular financing keeps AI companies afloat, what Chinese open-source models undercutting OpenAI and Anthropic mean for US workers, and why grassroots opposition to data centers is a reasonable response to hyperscale projects that drain power and water while creating few jobs. He warns of a 2008-style recession on steroids, and explains why following the money today matters more than the “shock message” of a coming AI apocalypse. Read Michael Roberts’ article “AI: The Biggest Bet in U.S. History”: https://thenextrecession.wordpress.com/2026/09/26/ai-the-biggest-economic-bet-in-us-history/ For more deep dives into the global economy, tech monopolies, and the real-world impact of AI – and to watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: [Speaker 1 (Zoe):] Is the US economy growing incredibly fast in the last year or is it a bubble that is about to burst? Tech giants like Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle are expected to pour more than four trillion into data centers, chips, and AI models by 2029. Brookings estimates total data center spending could reach 10.3 trillion by 2032. And that’s more relative to the GDP than railroads, the highway system, or the internet. Up to July, 37 billion has actually been spent on private data centers with most still not operating. In contrast, US private construction spending on everything else that it does, houses, apartment buildings, shopping centers, and so on was about 46 billion dollar below the levels in the year prior in the first seven months just of this year. So that’s a marked difference and a marked contrast. All of this is part of what experts have been referring to as the AI bubble. And so to discuss this, what does it mean for everyday people in the United States and the world, we are joined by Michael Roberts, socialist economist, author of several books on the world economy, and the author of a blog called The Next Recession. Thank you so much, Michael, for joining us today here on BT Live. [Speaker 2 (Michael Roberts):] Pleased to be with you, Zoe. An important matter to discuss, I think. [Speaker 1 (Zoe):] Extremely important. And your latest article, AI, the biggest bet in US history, was very important. We’re going to link it in the show notes because I highly recommend that everyone read this article. But of course in this article, you start out by saying that AI is the biggest economic bet in US history. As you report in this article, spending is set to pass 1 trillion next year. However, the free cash flow funding is falling below 100 billion. So, explain to us what does that gap mean? How does that impact ordinary people and is this something that we should be worried about? [Speaker 2 (Michael Roberts):] Well, it seems that American institutions, the financial institutions, companies, government are absolutely placing a huge bet on AI delivering faster growth for the United States, better wages for everybody, higher profits for companies. In fact, a whole new wonderful world is going to come from this AI, artificial intelligence. And that in order to do that they want to spend huge amounts and are spending huge amounts of money. Both the banks are lending money, private credit institutions are putting money into AI labs and into data centers dotted across the United States and there’s still more to come. This is a massive investment. Will it come off is the question. And also before it even does come off, will the money run out? Because already most of the money that’s been provided for this investment up to now has come from the profits from the big tech media companies who were making lots of profit from previous businesses, cloud businesses, internet businesses. Now they’re running out of how much money they can put in. So they’re now borrowing money. So the debt is rising to cover these AI investments which are taking place. And now within the next month or so, one of the big AI labs called Anthropic is going to launch a share issue where it wants to raise $2 trillion, a massive amount of money which it claims if it gets it will be able to deliver fantastic AI models that companies can use in every sort of part of their business and transform the situation, probably at the expense of a lot of jobs unfortunately for people who are currently working in them. [Speaker 1 (Zoe):] Well, I want to touch on something that you illustrate in the article with a slightly complicated graph, but you explain it very well, which is this concept of circular financing, and you explain how AI companies are essentially staying afloat because of this issue that you illustrated of lack of free cash flow funding. And you explain how firms are lending and buying from each other, and it seems that everyone is essentially dependent on each other’s spending. So can you exactly explain how this works and why is this actually a risk instead of a normal business practice? [Speaker 2 (Michael Roberts):] Well, it is in a way a normal business practice to lend money to companies in the hope that they will produce sales and revenues and that then they will get their money back. But that’s not the sort of lending that’s going on now. What’s happening is that the big companies in tech are lending money to the artificial intelligence labs as they’re called. The people who are making these models and these models are then claiming they’re making huge amounts of revenue. But the only way they’re making huge amounts of revenue is they’re getting loans from the other tech companies. So for example, Nvidia which makes all the chips for all these AI companies and for these data centers basically invested in all the AI companies and are lending the money to all the companies. So the result of course is that the companies appear to have plenty of cash but they have an obligation to deliver at some point huge amounts of revenues back to Nvidia. In the meantime this money keeps circulating around and we call it circular financing in the most complex way. That graph shows how much connection there is between all these different companies at all different levels not just in the US but right across the world now. And so if one company particularly a big one starts to lose confidence in making those investments or loses revenue and can’t achieve the targets that it has to make then the whole of this web could start to crumble and cause the bubble to burst and we see a massive reduction in the value of all these companies on the stock market and that will produce losses of jobs, losses of income for large numbers of people and we could then slip into a recession in the United States. That’s the risk. It’s so we have one huge bet now on the US economy that AI is going to work. It’s going to deliver huge profits for the companies that have made these loans and it’s going to deliver greater productivity for the economy as a whole. That’s a huge risky bet. [Speaker 1 (Zoe):] Well, you know, it’s interesting your piece comes out and we’re discussing it right now in the midst of this whole AI news crisis where we’ve seen several whistleblowers, so to speak, come forward and say, you know, AI could kill us all. AI could end humanity. We are racing towards a point of no return, talking about the possibilities that their AI models are unleashing on the people of the world. And it’s interesting because what you’re outlining in this article is that there’s a very real risk that will come before all of that, which is the economic impact. And so what do you think could be the fallout of any of this starting to collapse, whether it’s the circular financing or some of these investments not returning? [Speaker 2 (Michael Roberts):] Yeah. Well, I think an estimate was made by the IMF recently and they reckon that it could reduce the stock market value by up to 25%. It could knock back our national output in the US and in other major economies by four or 5%. If you remember the great recession that some of us remember back in 2008-2009 knocked about 3 or 4% off the national output of major economies for several years. This would be just as bad if not worse if we get into that situation. That’s the risk. Now I have to say that at the moment stock market investors, financial institutions, AI labs, the big tech companies are completely optimistic. That’s not going to happen. They say they’re going to be able to deliver much better models which companies can use right throughout their businesses, get rid of a lot of costs, and dramatically increase their productivity and therefore sell more goods and services, and it will transform the situation for the US. The chairman of the US Federal Reserve said this is the most important thing. It’s going to keep prices down. It’s going to increase productivity. It’s going to transform the economy. That’s the optimistic message that remains. Who actually mentioned, Zoe, the pessimistic message is it’s so powerful this AI apparently, it’s going to take over human beings’ jobs, but is actually going to control human beings and even annihilate them. I think that’s a sort of shock message which I think tells you two things: one is that the AI labs want to convince you that this is absolutely powerful and will work, and secondly, if it’s dangerous they’d like to slow down the process a little bit, so they want it both ways at the moment. They don’t want to spend too much more money. On the other hand, they want you to believe that it’s going to deliver. And that’s the big question we have now. So I could call it a $64,000 question, but what we’re talking about is a four or $5 trillion question, which is if you know that the US economy produces labor and machines produce about $30 trillion a year, you can see that if that happened the loss of $5 trillion every year for the next five years that would be a disaster for the US economy. [Speaker 1 (Zoe):] No, that’s duly noted. And you know, let’s talk about data centers a bit because in your piece you wrote about how $37 billion has been spent on private data centers, and notably you included a graph showing that a lot of these are not operational yet. And across the United States and in many parts of the world, the construction of data centers has been met with mass grassroots opposition. Recent polling in the United States shows that not only do progressives and Democrats oppose the construction of data centers in their neighborhoods and their areas, but it’s actually something that’s a bipartisan issue for voters. Even Republican voters have joined in this mass opposition to the construction of data centers. How does that factor play into this? Because again $37 billion, it’s not $4 trillion, but it’s still a significant amount. Will the grassroots opposition to the construction of these centers have an impact on how this is playing out in the economy? Is that—we’ve seen a lot of vilification by these tech billionaires against people who are protesting the data centers saying that they’re anti-American. Break down a bit of this for us. [Speaker 2 (Michael Roberts):] Well, there are genuine worries for people who have got data centers near them. Data centers consume huge amounts of water. Why is that? Because there are computers and chips buzzing away in these data centers, increasing dramatically the temperature of what’s going on inside. So, they need to be cooled all the time. So they need a large amount of water to keep cooling the center down so that nothing catches fire or breaks down. At the same time they’re using huge amounts of electricity. They’re sucking in electricity in order to keep these computers going. And this is obviously going to have an effect both on the power situation and the water situation in many parts of the country wherever these data centers have been built. And that’s a perfectly reasonable, genuine grievance that people have: do we need this massive expenditure that’s going on in these centers sucking away power and water for us? And remember, people are getting jobs by constructing them, but once they’re built they don’t really have many people working in them. So they’re not going to increase employment dramatically at all. Worse than that, Zoe, as you saw in that graph, large numbers of data centers that have been promised to be built haven’t been built. But companies have bought huge amounts of chips from Nvidia and other companies to put in these data centers because these semiconductor chips, that’s what really is going into them. And then they can’t put them in because the centers haven’t been built. So they’re sitting in warehouses just sitting there waiting to be used over the next 5 years maybe, because it takes about 3 to 5 years to complete a data center. So in that situation this is a real risk. Large amounts of money have been spent on computers, on chips, and started to construct data centers. But will people use them? Will companies use the AI models that are being produced to run their businesses and therefore use the data centers as a result? It remains to be seen. If they don’t, then there’s going to be a huge loss not only for companies that have invested in the data centers and the people looking to sell goods to people through the data centers, but also the people living next to the data centers will find that these things have been built for no reason whatsoever because they can’t deliver. [Speaker 1 (Zoe):] And you know, another aspect of this whole AI economy risk is the fact that the US is not the only country that is producing AI. It’s not only these US tech giants that are producing cutting-edge AI models, and you note the rise of Chinese open-source models, which are significantly cheaper in terms of the cost invested into creating them, but also the number of data centers etc. Overall, it’s a much cheaper investment in these open-source models, and this is overall driving prices down. And you refer to this as a classic contradiction, because there may be a rise in productivity, but the profits will also be kind of destroyed to be able to pay for this. So talk a bit more about this: what role do these open-source models play in this kind of drive to invest and this AI bubble in the United States? [Speaker 2 (Michael Roberts):] Two things. Open source means that basically if you’re a computer expert—not like me or you—you can go into the model and you can work out how it works, and you can get all the programs and algorithms out of it, and you can build your own model or use it for free. The models that the American companies are selling like Anthropic and OpenAI are not open source; you have to pay large amounts of money if you want to get control of that model—it’s proprietary and to use it. Also, that means that Chinese companies, but not just Chinese companies, but other open-source companies in France and in other parts of Europe can sell their time when you go and prompt an AI model. You buy a token to use something in your business or for your information, and they can sell their tokens at virtually nothing at all because they’re not really charging any money for the source models that they’ve produced. This undercuts the position of OpenAI and Anthropic dramatically. They’ve had to reduce their charges for tokens, as they’re called in this business, for information and algorithms that companies can use in their businesses. So there are two things here. Companies can set up their own open-source models to use in their companies; they don’t have to use OpenAI or Anthropic maybe, and also they can use the Chinese models or the open-source models very cheaply. So as you correctly say, this may improve the productivity of companies that are buying these things and using them, but it means that the profitability of the existing AI companies and the people who have made all these investments and loans to them may not be delivered as a result. [Speaker 1 (Zoe):] And you know, just before we let you go, I wanted to ask you one last question. It feels like we’re kind of on a precipice here, as you’ve laid out in terms of this bubble. What—of course you don’t have a crystal ball, neither do I—what should we be looking for in terms of triggering events which could change the current situation? It feels quite tenuous right now. What should people be paying attention to in terms of reports or things that could change this balance that you describe? [Speaker 2 (Michael Roberts):] Well, this boom, this bubble, if we want to call it that, could continue for another year, maybe longer—can’t be sure. So that’s why actually we can’t be sure. But what we should be looking for, for example, is if there’s suddenly a downturn in the demand to build more data centers, or if the share issue that Anthropic is making in November turns out to be a bit of a dud—they don’t raise the money they expect to do so, or if they raise the money then the price of the shares afterwards drops sharply. That would indicate a lack of confidence in the possibility of these AI models delivering what they claim they can deliver over the next few years. And if they don’t start changing the levels of productivity—if companies don’t adopt these AI models, and sometimes that can take a long time before they get round to doing it, putting it through their own companies and using it in an effective way—if that takes a long time, in the meantime all this money is being spent and it’s not getting a return, we will begin to see a fall in the profitability prospects for those companies and a withdrawal by the investors about making more investments. We see that beginning to happen. That tells you that the turn towards a bust from a boom in the AI stock market and elsewhere is beginning to happen. So it really depends on all of us, all the workers, company owners—not us, but—to embrace this for it not to be a boom-and-bust. So at the moment they are embracing it. Don’t worry there, if you go into the mainstream media, it’s going to be fantastic. And I hope they’re right in some ways. We don’t want massive numbers of jobs to be lost, we don’t want a huge decline in output or people’s incomes because of this bust. But as we know in the history of capitalism, in the history of stock markets, that’s what happens quite often. And the example at the very beginning of the show when you showed the railway mania that happened in the 19th century, that collapsed before we got the railways; the dotcom bubble collapsed in the early 2000s, then we got the internet. This time we could have a huge AI bubble that collapses. We may still be left with artificial intelligence machines afterwards that we can use, but it’s going to be at a cost to us all, not only in the US, but across the world. [Speaker 1 (Zoe):] Well, Michael Roberts, thank you so much for joining us here on BT Live. Definitely recommend to anyone who’s watching, please check out his piece, follow his blog; you will thank us later. So, Michael, thanks for being here. [Speaker 2 (Michael Roberts):] Thanks for having me.

articles.title: Ghana swiftly rejects US health deal, calls it ‘humiliating’
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Ghana has rejected a proposed health compact with the United States that would have provided an estimated $109 million in US health funding over five years, with President John Dramani Mahama saying the agreement raised serious concerns over health data, financing obligations, and Ghana’s regulatory authority. The decision places Ghana among a few African countries that have pushed back against new US health agreements introduced as Washington restructures its foreign assistance following the dismantling of USAID. Zimbabwe has also rejected a similar agreement, while Zambia has raised concerns over provisions in its negotiations with the United States. Ghana raises concerns over health data Speaking at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York on September 25, Mahama said the proposed compact was presented to Ghana as a replacement for health funding previously provided through USAID. He said Ghana’s Ministry of Health reviewed the document before preparing a Cabinet Information Paper. “Ghana is a sovereign nation, and we have our own processes. We are a democratic country,” Mahama said. According to the President, the Cabinet identified several provisions that raised concerns, particularly those relating to Ghana’s health information. “One, it says that we shall give the United States our pathogen profile,” he said, adding that the agreement also required Ghana to provide medical records. “It also says we should give our medical records. I mean, who takes another country’s medical records? And so that was strange.” Concerns over health-data sharing have been central to resistance to the new US health agreements in several African countries. No FDA inspection Mahama also raised concerns about the treatment of medicines and other medical products supplied under the proposed arrangement. He said Ghana would have been required to contribute funding to the program while, according to his account of the compact, the country’s Food and Drugs Authority would not have been able to inspect medicines or other medical products entering Ghana under the program. “And then it also says that any medications or any medical products that shall be brought into our country, our Food and Drugs Administration has absolutely no right to inspect,” Mahama said. “I mean, it was humiliating.” Ghanaian officials had previously cited concerns about the proposed handling of sensitive health information as a reason for rejecting the agreement. Reporting on the negotiations also indicated that the proposed arrangement would have required additional investment from Ghana alongside the US contribution. Cabinet rejected the agreement Mahama said the proposal was rejected after the Health Ministry presented its assessment to the Cabinet. He described the decision as unusually swift. “It was the compact that was thrown out in record time in our Cabinet. I’ve never seen anything thrown out as fast as that.” He said the government subsequently instructed the Health Minister to communicate Ghana’s position to the US ambassador. “And so, of course, we rejected it. And we asked the health minister to inform the US ambassador that we didn’t need it. We’ll manage ourselves.” The proposed agreement would have provided Ghana with about $109 million in US health assistance over five years. The negotiations had begun in late 2025. A wider concern over health sovereignty Ghana’s decision comes as the United States seeks to shift its approach to global health cooperation. The new US strategy places greater emphasis on recipient countries taking responsibility for financing and delivering health programs, while Washington reduces its traditional aid commitments. Kenya became the first African country to sign the agreement which was challenged in court, followed by similar arrangements with Rwanda, Liberia, Uganda, Lesotho and Eswatini, among other countries. Ravi Ram from the People’s Health Movement (PHM) East and South Africa, told BreakThrough News in December 2025, that “Bilateral agreements between the US and Kenya and other African countries are meant to limit the ability of any one ‘partner’ country to challenge the terms of implementing the agreement, due to the unequal power relations.” The concerns among health activists and concerned Africans is the ability of African states to determine their own health priorities, regulate medicines, control sensitive health information, and collectively negotiate the terms of international health cooperation.

articles.title: China’s rise: from Century of Humiliation to global superpower w/ Ken Hammond
articles.author: Amanda Yee
articles.content: On October 1, 1949, Mao Zedong stood in Tiananmen Square and declared the founding of the People’s Republic of China, bringing an end to the “Century of Humiliation” and setting a nation representing a quarter of humanity on a path toward self-determination. Seventy-seven years later, China stands as a global superpower, navigating a rapidly shifting multipolar world order and escalating containment pressures from the United States. Professor of East Asian and global history Dr. Ken Hammond joins Amanda Yee to break down the historical, economic, and geopolitical forces that have shaped modern China’s development and foreign policy over the past 77 years.

articles.title: Prosecutor leading investigation of Cerimedo arrested by Bolivian police, days after facing US sanctions
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: On the evening of Wednesday, September 30, Bolivian police arrested Attorney General Roger Mariaca and raided the Attorney General’s Office in Sucre and Santa Cruz. The police action comes just days after the US State Department sanctioned and revoked the visas of Mariaca and 21 other Bolivians. Analysts suggest that the timing of the US sanctions, Mariaca’s arrest, and the raids, are no coincidence, calling it “political pressure” related to a high-profile case. Mariaca is leading the investigation into Argentine political consultant Fernando Cerimedo. The influential political advisor to Latin America’s far right allegedly influenced elections through social media bot farms, may be involved in drug trafficking, and was accused of ordering an assassination attempt on his ex-partner, Nadia Beller. She was shot three times but survived after undergoing emergency surgery. Cerimedo has been in custody in Bolivia after attempting to leave the country by plane following the attack on Beller. Messages were found on his cell phone that, according to the prosecution, directly link him to the attempt on her life. Despite the emerging evidence against him, not only in ordering the hit on Beller, but also in crimes of corruption and drug trafficking, Cerimedo seems to have friends in high places, both in the Bolivian president’s office, and in the United States, that may have set the stage for the arrest of his investigator, Attorney General Roger Mariaca. Read more: Attempted murder accusations, troll farms, and presidential connections: the notorious case of Fernando Cerimedo Argentine outlet Página 12 , reported that, according to Beller, the sanctions against Mariaca were “a move by Donald Trump’s team to protect Cerimedo. As the Washington Post noted this week: ‘Cerimedo is the MAGA (Make America Great Again, Trump’s slogan) man across the entire continent.’” In the report, Beller is quoted as saying : “Is this decision by the United States part of the fight for the Shield of the Americas or is it about protecting the MAGA network?…If the reason is corruption and drug trafficking, then they need to explain why the visa is being revoked for the attorney general who is investigating a network of that nature. Are they going after the investigator, or are they protecting part of the network?” As evidence mounts against Cerimedo, the US instead accused his investigator, Mariaca, of allegedly soliciting and accepting bribes to facilitate drug trafficking and helping people involved in violent crimes escape justice. After news broke of the US actions against him, Roger Mariaca had said he will not back down and will continue the investigations until the end: “[I received the news] with great surprise … I will not back down even one centimeter from the investigations that fall under my jurisdiction.” He highlighted that while it is clear that the Cerimedo case has generated international intrigue, “no political pressure, whether national or international, can become an impediment to clarifying the facts which must be investigated.” He was arrested two days later. Involvement in the drug trade? In addition to Cerimedo’s well-documented ties to high profile right-wing politicians across Latin America, including in Bolivia, recent revelations from ex-partner Beller, suggest that the powerful political consultant may have also been involved in the drug trade. In a leaked audio message, Cerimedo is allegedly speaking with a woman with whom he is arranging payment so that several flights can operate without excessive pressure from the authorities. Cerimedo mentions a man named Cabrera, whom the Bolivian media suspect is Franz Cabrera, the former head of the Special Force to Fight Against Drug Trafficking (FELCN), who was recently dismissed. According to the investigations , they allegedly “were paid” for nearly 45 flights, amounting to $700,000, raising significant suspicions about the source of the funds that the political consultant is said to have handled. The timing of the sanctions against Mariaca and his arrest have raised questions about US interference in the Bolivian justice system. But, as pressure escalates over the investigation into Cerimedo, the case is also revealing a far deeper web of political connection and influence than was initially known, placing it under renewed scrutiny. Wether the investigation is further disrupted or allowed to proceed, what happens next could expose even more about Cerimedo and the network of the Latin American far right.
